channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: Japan's corporate goods price index rose 6.8% in the year to September, below the 7.6% median forecast, as firms passed on chemical and fuel costs, and the yen-based import price index rose 24.5%, CNA reports.
item.description:
CNA reports that, in data released on 13 October, Japan's wholesale prices, measured by the corporate goods price index of what companies charge each other for goods and services, rose 6.8% in the year to September against a median market forecast of 7.6%, as firms passed on chemical and fuel costs. The yen-based import price index rose 24.5% year on year in September, which the report reads as a sign that the weak currency continued to push up the cost of imported raw materials. The summary does not give the monthly change, the split between chemical and fuel costs or the August figure.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The index measures prices between companies, so it shows cost pass-through along supply chains and not consumer prices. On a general reading rather than on anything in the source, costs passed on by chemical and fuel suppliers raise costs for the manufacturers who use them, and a weak currency adds to the yen price of imported raw materials. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, producers in Japan face higher costs for chemical and fuel inputs, and a weaker yen reduces the yen value of sales by exporters to Japan. Points that may be worth considering include whether the next release shows further pass-through, how the yen moves, and whether chemical prices lead or follow fuel prices.

CNA

item.title: The IMF's World Economic Outlook puts 2026 world growth at 3.1%, with AI investment offsetting the energy shock from the Middle East war, and warns the global economy "could soon test the limits of resilience".
item.description:
The IMF's twice-yearly World Economic Outlook, released at its Bangkok meetings, puts world growth at 3.1% in 2026, AP and The Straits Times report, and says AI investment is offsetting the damage from sharply higher oil and gas prices. The Guardian reports that the IMF said growth withstood the Middle East conflict better than feared and that releases of strategic energy stocks and the rerouting of oil supplies away from the Strait of Hormuz helped contain the impact on oil prices, but that emergency stocks are now depleted and high debts and deficits could leave governments little capacity to protect consumers from a further price jump. AP adds that the benefits are unevenly shared, with the US and China accounting for more than three-quarters of net demand for AI-related equipment and 32 countries for 95% of global growth. By economy: advanced economies 2.1% in 2026 and 1.9% in 2027; the US 2.3% in both years; the euro area 1.1% in 2026 and 1.2% in 2027, with forecasts raised for its main members except France; the UK 1.3% in 2026, up from 1%, and 1.2% in 2027; China 4.5% in 2026, lowered from July, and 4.0% in 2027; India 7% in 2026, up from 6.4%. MarketScreener adds that a longer war would lower growth and raise inflation. The reporting does not give a 2027 world figure on which the sources agree or a figure for Germany.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The outlook combines a forecast with a risk assessment: the 3.1% is an estimate, and the warning about depleted stocks and debt is the fund's judgement. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, growth that rests on AI investment in a few economies leaves other sectors, including construction and consumer goods, dependent on the energy and interest-rate outlook, and depleted oil stocks mean a new supply disruption would meet less of a buffer. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, the regional split matters: India's higher forecast and the euro area's modest growth set the demand backdrop for construction and manufacturing customers, and China's lower forecast bears on one of the largest end-markets. Points that may be worth considering include how the regional forecasts move at the next revision, how energy prices develop if oil stocks stay low, and whether the AI-investment contribution persists.

AP | The Straits Times | The Guardian | Le Parisien | BBC News | New Indian Express | The Economic Times | MarketScreener

item.title: China's finance ministry and tax administration will cut the export tax rebate on new energy vehicles from 13% to 9% from April 2027, which Bernstein analysts read as primarily aimed at curbing industry "involution".
item.description:
MarketScreener reports that China's Ministry of Finance and State Taxation Administration announced the cut of the export tax rebate for new energy vehicles (NEVs) from 13% to 9%, effective April 2027. It cites Bernstein analysts, who say the reduction is primarily intended to curb industry "involution" and promote consolidation in favour of stronger, more disciplined carmakers, and who say that with lower rebates Chinese carmakers will need to recalibrate their export strategies, can no longer simply replicate low-priced models for overseas markets and will have to decide whether to absorb the extra cost or pass it on to buyers. The report does not say whether plug-in hybrids are covered, what the rebate refunds, how the cut compares with other products, or what the authorities give as the purpose; the purpose and the effects are Bernstein's reading.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The source gives the rate change and the date, and the stated purpose is the analysts' reading, so the authorities' own reason is not reported. On a general reading rather than on anything in the source, "involution" is the term used in China for price competition that squeezes margins across an industry, and an export tax rebate is typically a refund of tax on goods sold abroad, so a lower rebate raises the cost of exporting. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, a higher export cost for Chinese vehicles could slow export growth or lead to more assembly abroad, and either would shift where bonding, sealing and battery materials are bought. Points that may be worth considering include whether export prices of Chinese vehicles change before April 2027, whether exports are brought forward, and whether other products see rebate cuts.

MarketScreener

item.title: Four Republican and three Democratic US senators say the diesel deal with Russia violates US law on Russian energy imports, and Wirtschaftswoche reports that an analysis of shipping data shows no effect so far.
item.description:
Herald Scotland (USA Today) reports that Trump said in a post that Russia will supply the US and global markets with 300,000 tons of diesel immediately, with more to follow, and that the Kremlin confirmed Russia's readiness to supply oil and petroleum products, and LiveMint reports that the announcement followed a conversation with Vladimir Putin. On 11 October, four Republican and three Democratic senators issued a joint statement calling on Trump to withdraw the agreement, saying Congress banned Russian energy imports in 2022 and that the administration neither consulted Congress nor gave the explanation the law requires, Lianhe Zaobao reports. Republican senator Thom Tillis said on NBC that the deal may be illegal. LiveMint reports that Trump defended the move by arguing that European countries had continued to pay Russia substantial sums for energy. Wirtschaftswoche reports that an analysis of shipping data showed no effect so far, that Russia's diesel exports are sharply reduced by Ukrainian drone attacks, and that Iranian attacks on tankers hold back extra supply to the US. The reporting does not say what the law requires for an exemption, whether the sanctions easing will be reversed, or how much Russian diesel is shipping.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The senators' objection concerns whether the easing stands and the shipping data concern whether any extra supply has arrived, so neither yet shows a change in diesel volumes. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, an easing that is legally contested can be narrowed or withdrawn, which makes the volumes it promises uncertain for traders planning cargoes, and price moves driven by announcements can reverse if supply does not follow. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, diesel is part of freight and distribution costs for raw materials and finished goods, so if the relief does not arrive, those costs stay exposed to the wider supply picture. Points that may be worth considering include whether Congress acts on the senators' objection, whether shipping data show Russian cargoes reaching the US, and how diesel prices respond if they do not.

Lianhe Zaobao | Herald Scotland | The Times of India | LiveMint | Wirtschaftswoche | Lianhe Zaobao

item.title: US agricultural tractor sales fell 16.4% and combine sales 10.9% year on year in September, and Canadian sales fell 15.1% and 37.6%, the Association of Equipment Manufacturers reports.
item.description:
The Association of Equipment Manufacturers (AEM) reports that sales of agricultural tractors in the US fell 16.4% year on year in September 2026 and combine sales fell 10.9%. In Canada, tractor sales fell 15.1% and combine sales 37.6%. The summary does not give unit numbers, the split by tractor size, year-to-date totals, the cause of the fall or any comment on farm incomes. It comes from one association release.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The release measures machine sales in one month and two countries, so it indicates farm-equipment demand in the US and Canada and not the level of farm activity. On a general reading rather than on anything in the source, lower equipment sales can reflect weak farm income, high financing costs or buyers waiting, and they reduce orders for the components and materials used in machines. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, agricultural and construction machinery use sealing, bonding and coating materials in cabs, panels and assemblies, so lower machine sales could reduce demand from that customer group. Points that may be worth considering include whether the October figures extend the decline, whether the pattern appears in construction equipment, and how the year-to-date totals look.

Association of Equipment Manufacturers

item.title: PwC's first Global Automotive Outlook, a survey of 720 executives in 33 countries, expects gasoline and diesel vehicles to fall from 60% to 41% of global production in five years and battery-electric vehicles to rise from 18% to 30%.
item.description:
El Correo reports on the first edition of PwC's Global Automotive Outlook, based on a survey of 720 executives from manufacturers and suppliers in 33 countries. Respondents expect the share of gasoline and diesel vehicles in production to fall from 60% to 41% in five years and the share of battery-electric vehicles to rise from 18% to 30%. By region, China's battery-electric share is expected to go from 29% to 40% of its production while combustion falls from 43% to 29%; in the US combustion remains the majority at 51%, down from 67%, with electric vehicles rising more modestly to 25%; Germany and Japan are expected to reach 41% and 40% combustion, with hybrids and pure electric both gaining; India is put at 48% combustion. The summary does not say what the remaining share is made of, when the survey was carried out, or how respondents are weighted by region.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The figures are executives' expectations, so they measure what respondents expect and not what has been produced. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a shift from combustion to battery-electric changes the materials in each vehicle, because battery packs and electric drive systems use different bonding, sealing and thermal-management materials from engines and exhausts. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, a faster electric shift in China and a slower one in the US would move demand for battery-related materials between regions, and combustion shares of about 40% in Germany and Japan leave room for mixed platforms. Points that may be worth considering include how actual 2026 production compares with the survey's starting shares, which regions revise their expectations, and how hybrids are counted.

El Correo

item.title: Chancellor Friedrich Merz vows to cut the electricity tax for all consumers to the EU minimum once higher growth expectations produce the budget room, which MarketScreener says could be roughly EUR 5 billion if projections hold.
item.description:
On 12 October, after a meeting of his conservatives on how to answer voters' concerns following heavy losses in state elections, Merz said budget room should be used to lower the electricity tax for everyone to the European minimum, as the coalition had originally promised, MarketScreener and the Frankfurter Allgemeine report. So far the tax has been lowered only for certain sectors of the economy. The cut had been planned for last year and dropped for lack of budget room. Handelsblatt reports Merz saying it should come as soon as higher growth expectations translate into higher tax revenue. The Frankfurter Allgemeine says he cited the government's forecast of 1.3% growth this year and the OECD forecast of 1.1% for 2027, and MarketScreener says that if the growth projections hold, roughly EUR 5 billion of additional federal tax revenue could result, precisely the amount needed. The reporting does not give the current and minimum tax rates, a start date, or whether rates for industry would change.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The pledge depends on growth lifting revenue, so it is a stated intention and not a decided measure. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a cut to the EU minimum would lower power costs for consumers, and the sources do not say whether businesses are covered, and a pledge tied to forecasts depends on later budget decisions. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, electricity is a cost in energy-intensive production steps and in customers' plants, so a lower tax could ease costs where reduced rates do not already apply, while an uncertain timetable limits how far it can be relied on. Points that may be worth considering include whether the growth forecasts hold, how the cut is fitted into the budget, and which consumers and sectors it covers.

MarketScreener | MarketScreener | Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung | Handelsblatt

item.title: ACEA reports that global new-car registrations were 35.7 million in the first half of 2026, down 4.9%, with China down 23.2% and the EU up 5.7%, and global production down 1% to 37.6 million.
item.description:
The European Automobile Manufacturers' Association (ACEA), in its report on the global and EU auto industry for the first half of 2026, says registrations fell mainly because of weaker domestic demand in China and lower registrations in the Middle East and Africa. It says EU registrations rose 5.7%, supported by strong demand incentives and pricing strategies, Asia declined by 11%, and South America grew fastest at 16.9%, driven largely by Brazil at 22.8%. Global car production fell 1% to 37.6 million units, with most major markets recording subdued output; China's production fell 5.8%, the first fall since 2020, and the country is increasingly focusing on export markets. The summary does not state the comparison period for the changes and does not give figures for the US, Japan or India, a monthly profile or a forecast for the second half.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The report is a half-year measure of registrations and production from the industry's own association, so it describes volumes already recorded and not a forecast. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, weaker Chinese demand with Chinese production turning to exports moves supply toward other regions, and the EU's incentive-led growth depends on those incentives continuing. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, registrations and production set demand for bonding, sealing and coating materials, so weaker Chinese output and stronger EU and South American registrations would move demand between regions. Points that may be worth considering include the second-half registration trend in China, whether EU demand incentives continue, and whether Chinese export volumes keep rising.

ACEA

item.title: The European Commission says Chinese hybrid and plug-in hybrid exports to the EU will be limited to 350,000 a year for four years from December, and officials estimate plug-in hybrid sales from China could reach about 800,000 in 2026, Tagesschau reports.
item.description:
On 9 October, EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič announced an agreement with China's Commerce Minister in Beijing as part of a wider trade package, the Association of European Vehicle Logistics reports. The Guardian reports that the Commission has confirmed a limit of 350,000 hybrid cars a year imported from China, to come into force in December under a four-year agreement, to be taken under World Trade Organization safeguard measures, which the paper says can be implemented without the investigations that anti-dumping duties need. Tagesschau, citing a Commission representative, gives the ceiling as 350,000 a year and says that once it is reached European customs authorities will no longer approve hybrid cars from China, and that Commission officials estimate plug-in hybrid sales from China could rise to about 800,000 in 2026; Les Echos describes the cap as less than half of that. The South China Morning Post reports that China will not retaliate, that it will cut tariffs on various European goods and that the cap rises 6% a year, a detail the other reports do not give. The News International describes a preliminary understanding between the EU and China with an upward adjustment of hybrid exports based on 2025 figures. The Association of European Vehicle Logistics says Šefčovič was not referring to the current import level, which it puts at around 50,000 hybrids and plug-in hybrids a month. The reporting does not say how the cap is allocated among carmakers or how large the Chinese tariff cuts are.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The cap figures are the Commission's account and one report describes a preliminary understanding, so the final terms are not yet public. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a quota under safeguard rules limits volume and not only price, so it changes how importers and carmakers plan their supply, and it can lead exporters to assemble inside the EU. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, hybrid cars use the same bonding, sealing and battery materials as other vehicles, so a shift of hybrid assembly from China to the EU would change where those materials are bought. Points that may be worth considering include how the cap is allocated between producers, whether Chinese carmakers respond with EU assembly, and what EU leaders say about the deal at their summit.

The Guardian | Les Echos | Tagesschau | South China Morning Post | The News International | The Association of European Vehicle Logistics | MarketScreener

item.title: Ifo finds that 14.6% of German industrial companies reported a lack of intermediate products in September, up from 13.3% in August, and 37.8% in data-processing, electronic and optical products, Handelsblatt reports.
item.description:
Handelsblatt reports on a survey by the Ifo Institute in Munich in which 14.6% of companies in German industry said in September that they lacked intermediate products, up from 13.3% in August. Supply is described as particularly tight for makers of data-processing equipment and of electronic and optical products, where the share of companies with material shortages rose from 33.2% to 37.8%. The reporting does not give shares for other branches such as chemicals, vehicles or machinery, does not say which intermediate products are scarce or what causes the shortages, and does not say whether production or orders were affected. The figure is a share of companies reporting a shortage, so it does not measure how large the shortage is for each of them.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The survey counts companies that report a shortage, so it indicates how widespread the problem is and not how severe it is. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, shortages in electronics are often tied to chips and components bought worldwide, and a rising share can signal supply-chain strain at customers of material suppliers. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, electronics makers use bonding, coating and sealing materials, so shortages at those customers can slow their output and ordering, and the sources do not show whether shortages extend to other branches. Points that may be worth considering include whether the October survey shows the share rising further, which branches follow electronics, and whether shortages begin to show in production data.

Handelsblatt

item.title: Volkswagen's global vehicle sales fell 14.3% year on year in the third quarter, after declines of 8.6% in the second quarter and 4.0% at the beginning of 2026, with China down 38.5%, Handelsblatt reports.
item.description:
Handelsblatt reports that Volkswagen delivered just over 6 million vehicles in the first nine months of 2026, 9.0% or around 600,000 fewer than a year earlier, and that the decline widened from 4.0% at the beginning of 2026 to 8.6% in the second quarter and 14.3% in the third. In China, deliveries were just under 406,000 in the third quarter, down 38.5%, and 1.38 million in nine months, down 30.2%. The report says Volkswagen is struggling in China with a declining overall market, strong price pressure and growing competition from domestic manufacturers, and that in Europe one in five models delivered in the nine months was a pure electric car. Anadolu reports that Audi's global deliveries were 1.04 million vehicles in nine months, down 11.4%, with third-quarter deliveries down 19.7% to 314,900, which it attributes to a market contraction in China, and third-quarter fully electric deliveries down 21.5% to 48,700. The reporting does not give a split by other brands, by regions outside China and Europe or by drive type beyond the European electric share, and does not give a forecast for the fourth quarter.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The figures are the sales of one group, so they show how much one large customer of the vehicle industry is selling, and the decline is steepest in China. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, lower vehicle volumes reduce demand for the materials used in each vehicle, and a shift of volume between regions changes where those materials are bought. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, vehicle assembly uses structural bonding, sealing and battery materials, so a fall in Volkswagen's China deliveries could reduce demand there and in Europe one in five models delivered being pure electric is one factor in demand elsewhere. Points that may be worth considering include whether the fourth-quarter decline in China narrows, how the European electric share develops, and how other German carmakers' third-quarter figures compare.

Handelsblatt | Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung | Anadolu Agency

item.title: US Energy Secretary Chris Wright says oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz have recovered to 80–90% of pre-conflict levels, but refined-product flows out of the Gulf are at only 25–35%, worsening diesel, jet fuel and gasoline shortages.
item.description:
Asharq Al-Awsat reports that Wright put oil flows through the strait at 80% to 90% of pre-conflict levels, averaging 13 million to 14 million barrels a day, and said substantial inventories and spare production capacity had kept crude supplies at manageable levels. The larger challenge, he said, is refined petroleum products leaving the Arabian Gulf, at 25% to 35% of pre-conflict levels, which worsens shortages of diesel, jet fuel and gasoline. He hoped higher output from Chinese refineries, which have spare capacity and attractive margins, would help, and said US refineries were processing crude and producing products at record levels. The Straits Times reports Brent below USD 106 a barrel after a rise of more than 6% over three sessions, with oil up more than 70% in 2026, and says Saudi Arabia is moving to reduce its reliance on the strait, with Aramco planning extra export capacity soon and a bigger bypass pipeline within two to three years. Aramco's chief executive, Amin Nasser, said continued disruption is intensifying pressure on crude and refined products, particularly diesel, and that commercial inventories offer only a limited buffer. The reporting does not say how the flow figures were measured, which period "pre-conflict" covers, or how product flows split between diesel, jet fuel and gasoline.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The sources contrast a largely recovered oil flow through the strait with a still-low flow of refined products out of the Gulf, so the shortage Wright describes sits mainly in refined products, while Aramco's chief executive describes pressure on both crude and refined products. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a product shortage can keep diesel prices and refining margins high even when crude is available, and naphtha, which comes from the same refineries, is a starting material for many plastics and chemical intermediates. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, fuel and logistics costs enter the delivered price of raw materials, and a prolonged product squeeze can also tighten supply of petrochemical-based raw materials used in resins and solvents. Points that may be worth considering include whether Gulf product exports move toward the crude recovery, how Chinese refinery output develops, and whether the Saudi bypass plans change the exposure to the strait.

Asharq Al-Awsat | The Straits Times | Asharq Al-Awsat
